title: Every other door
hook: leaving every other door, I have come to Yours; keep my honor (Chaupai, dohra)

segments.voice: Yesterday, charan, and your line, held at the feet. This week: ichhaa, the enemy within, carry them across, spread and gathered, he knows the pain, held at the feet. Today, the very last couplet. Day three hundred seventy-eight.

Count the doors you've knocked on in your life. Literal ones: the job interviews, the landlord, the new neighbor. And the other kind: the friend you hoped would understand, the qualification you hoped would make you enough, the achievement that was going to fix everything. Some opened. Some didn't. Some opened onto rooms that turned out to be empty. Most people have a long list of doors behind them. Chaupai ends with someone standing at the end of that list, having tried them all, and standing now at one last door. Today: duaar.
screen: `ALL THE DOORS YOU'VE KNOCKED ON.` → `SOME OPENED ONTO EMPTY ROOMS.` → `ONE LAST DOOR.`

segments.voice: The closing couplet, a dohra, goes like this in paraphrase: leaving every other door, I have taken hold of your door. You who have taken my arm, keep my honor. Gobind is your servant. Duaar means door. Sagal duaar, every door. Tuhaaro duaar, your door. And there's that picture from day three hundred seventy-one: baanh gahe, the one who has taken my arm. In Punjabi, to take someone's arm is a promise of protection, the kind you don't walk away from. So the couplet says: you made a promise when you took my arm; keep it, keep my honor. Laaj, the word for honor here, is close to a sense of dignity and good name. It's a very human thing to ask. Don't let me be shamed. And then the signature. Gobind is your servant. This is Guru Gobind Singh, signing the last line of his prayer not as Guru, not as leader of the Khalsa, but as Gobind das, the servant. It's the same humility as yesterday's line, I have not said this. Notice the sequence. The prayer began with a hand. Protect me, giving me your hand. It ends with an arm, taken. The heart's wish was to stay at the feet. It ends at the door, having left every other. A whole prayer, and it's really one movement: a person walking past every other option to the one place they want to be kept. Some Sikhs say this couplet on its own in moments of fear, as if it carried the whole Chaupai in two lines.
screen: `LEAVING EVERY OTHER DOOR.` · `YOU WHO TOOK MY ARM, KEEP MY HONOR.` · `GOBIND IS YOUR SERVANT.` · `FROM A HAND TO AN ARM, TO A DOOR.` · then, large: `YOUR DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand still at a doorway. Get up, if you can, and go stand in an open doorway in your home. Stand right in the frame. Feel the threshold under your feet. Behind you, one room. In front, another. Breathe slowly. Think of the doors you've knocked on, the ones that opened and the ones that didn't. Then let them go, one by one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, standing at this door. If you don't, just notice how it feels to stop knocking and simply stand. The bell holds the time.
Duaar, door. Chaupai's last couplet: leaving every other door I have come to yours; you who took my arm, keep my honor. Gobind is your servant.
Your line: your door. Today, before you knock on a door you're counting on, a call, a request, a hope, notice what you're asking it to give you. Day three hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this closing dohra as part of Chaupai Sahib and Rehras, and some say it on its own in moments of fear as a short prayer for protection.

fork.setup: you've knocked on every door there is: wealth, praise, power, people. you're at the last one. what does Chaupai's couplet say?
options: leaving every other door, I have taken hold of yours; keep my honor.
fork.reveal: sagal duaar kau chhaad kai gahio tuhaaro duaar: leaving every door, I hold yours. and then, Gobind is your servant.

original.note: Gurmukhi: duaar, door; in Chaupai's last couplet, every other door left behind for one.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about choosing one religion over others.
what it means: a person who has tried every other door stands at the Lord's door and asks to be kept, signed Gobind, your servant.
what a scholar hears: baanh gahe kee laaj, the honor of the one who has taken my arm, uses the Punjabi idiom of a binding promise of protection, closing the hand image the prayer opened with.
